cards.headline: Words named after people
lines: 'Sandwich' is named after John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, in the 1700s.
'Boycott' comes from Captain Charles Boycott, shunned by his community in Ireland in 1880.
'Diesel' honours the engineer Rudolf Diesel.
cards.source: Oxford English Dictionary, etymologies of 'sandwich', 'boycott' and 'diesel'.

cards.headline: English is a great borrower
lines: English grew from the Germanic speech of the Anglo-Saxons.
After 1066, thousands of French words arrived — beef, court, justice.
Latin and Greek later supplied much of the vocabulary of science.
cards.source: Crystal, 'The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the English Language'; Baugh & Cable, 'A History of the English Language'.

cards.headline: Why 'cow' in the field but 'beef' on the plate?
lines: After the Norman Conquest, French words like 'beef' and 'pork' entered English and, over time, came to mean the meat.
The English words kept the animal — a split likely helped by French-speaking elites' tables.
cards.source: Baugh & Cable, 'A History of the English Language'; Crystal, 'The Stories of English'.

cards.headline: A few words do most of the work
lines: In English text, 'the' is the most common word.
Zipf noticed a pattern: the 2nd most common word appears about half as often as the 1st, the 3rd about a third as often.
Learning a language? The most frequent words pay off first.

visual.caption: Zipf's law: word rank vs. how often it appears

cards.source: Zipf, 'Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort' (1949).

cards.headline: About 7,000 languages are spoken today
lines: Ethnologue lists roughly 7,000 living languages.
Around 40% of them are endangered, many with fewer than 1,000 speakers.
When a language disappears, so does a unique way of describing the world.
cards.source: Ethnologue: Languages of the World (SIL International), recent editions.

cards.question: Which word is a palindrome?
cards.why: A palindrome reads the same backwards: L-E-V-E-L.

cards.question: 'Buzz', 'sizzle' and 'thud' are examples of…
cards.why: Onomatopoeia: words that imitate the sound they describe.
cards.source: Baldick, 'The Oxford Dictionary of Literary Terms'.

cards.question: Which phrase is an oxymoron?
cards.why: An oxymoron pairs contradictory words for effect: silence can't literally be deafening.
cards.source: Baldick, 'The Oxford Dictionary of Literary Terms'.

cards.question: Which language has the most native speakers?
cards.why: Mandarin has the most native speakers. Count second-language speakers too, and English has the most overall.

cards.question: Where does the word 'alphabet' come from?
options: The name of a Phoenician king
cards.why: Alpha and beta — letters that themselves descend from Phoenician aleph and beth.
cards.source: Oxford English Dictionary, 'alphabet'; Daniels & Bright, 'The World's Writing Systems'.

cards.headline: The dot over an 'i' is called a tittle
cards.text: The word comes from Latin 'titulus'. The old phrase 'every jot and tittle' means every tiny detail.

cards.headline: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog'
cards.text: It uses every letter of the alphabet — a pangram — and has long been used to test typewriters and fonts.

cards.headline: Shakespeare is the first recorded user of many words
cards.text: The Oxford English Dictionary's earliest citations for words like 'lonely' and 'eyeball' come from his plays — though some were likely spoken earlier.
cards.source: Oxford English Dictionary, first citations; Crystal, 'Think on My Words' (2008).

cards.headline: Babies can hear sounds from any language
cards.text: Young infants can tell apart speech sounds from many languages. By about their first birthday, they tune in to the sounds of the languages around them.
cards.source: Werker & Tees (1984), Infant Behavior and Development; Kuhl (2004), Nature Reviews Neuroscience.

cards.headline: Four main ways to write a language

steps.headline: 1 · Alphabets
lines: Letters stand for individual sounds — consonants and vowels.
Greek, Latin and Cyrillic are alphabets.

steps.headline: 2 · Abjads
lines: Letters mostly stand for consonants; readers supply many of the vowels.
Arabic and Hebrew are usually written this way.
Abugidas, like Hindi's Devanagari, write consonants with vowel marks attached.

steps.headline: 3 · Syllabaries
lines: Each symbol stands for a whole syllable.
Japanese kana and the Cherokee syllabary are examples.

steps.headline: 4 · Logographic
lines: Characters stand for words or meaningful parts of words.
Chinese characters work this way, often combining clues to meaning and sound.

cards.headline: Language & words: the takeaways
points: Many words are named after people.
English borrowed heavily from French and Latin.
Cow in the field, beef on the plate.
A few common words do most of the work.
